exercises.title: Three orders, one line moved
exercises.task: Read the three functions: they are the same except for where the node itself is visited. Run prints the three orders for the tree 4 2 6 1 3 5 7 and for your old A B C D tree.

exercises.title: Evaluate an expression tree
exercises.task: 3 × (4 + (5 − 1)) as a tree: operators inside, numbers at the leaves. Fill Eval (post-order: both sides first, then the operator) and Infix (in-order: left, operator, right, with brackets).
hints: A leaf (n.Op == 0) is just its number. Otherwise evaluate n.Left and n.Right, then apply n.Op.
Infix of a leaf is strconv.Itoa(n.Num); of an operator: "(" + Infix(left) + " " + string(n.Op) + " " + Infix(right) + ")".
switch n.Op { case '+': … }: Op is a rune, so compare with '+', not "+".

exercises.title: Build order and dismantle order
exercises.task: Given a directory tree (here, the source of a small compiler), return the paths in the order to create them (a directory before what is inside it) and in the order to delete them (what is inside before the directory). Children are visited in the order given. This is what mkdir -p and rm -r do inside the file system: rmdir refuses a directory that is not empty.
hints: Create: pre-order (the node, then its children). Delete: post-order (the children, then the node).
Pass the parent's path down: a child's path is parent + "/" + name; the root's path is its name.
A recursive helper that appends to a *[]string, or returns a slice that the caller appends.
